profiles.meeting_scenario: An ML research brainstorming meeting between a faculty lead and a senior PhD student who are shaping a workshop paper on activation functions. They want to move beyond a generic survey and brainstorm a sharper contribution around 'comparison of trends in practice and research' for deep learning activation functions. The immediate context is that they have one week to settle the paper angle before assigning a literature sweep and lightweight empirical checks. The agenda is to generate candidate framings for what counts as 'practice', what evidence they can credibly assemble, and how to define a contribution that looks novel without requiring a full benchmark campaign. The expected outcome is an agreed high-level paper concept, a shortlist of evidence sources to mine, and a rough plan for what supporting analysis to run.

members.name: Dr. Maya Srinivasan
members.expertise: Deep learning methodology, empirical ML papers, benchmark design
members.background: Leads a university ML systems-and-methods lab and has published survey-style and empirical synthesis papers on model design choices across vision and language tasks.
members.private_state: She wants a paper angle that is publishable as a methods-oriented synthesis, looks more rigorous than a narrative survey, and can be executed quickly by the lab without negotiating external industry data access.
hidden_assumptions: If they say 'practice', it can be operationalized through widely used open-source training code and public model repositories because that is the only scalable evidence base.
A 'trend' should mean a temporally visible shift over multiple years rather than a static frequency snapshot.
A contribution is 'lightweight empirically validated' if it includes a few controlled sanity-check reruns showing activation choices are often inherited defaults rather than actively tuned.
When discussing 'deployment-ready recommendations', the scope naturally excludes hardware-specific inference engineering details unless they are already reflected in common training repositories.

members.name: Leo Martinez
members.expertise: Literature mining, reproducibility studies, industry-facing applied deep learning
members.background: Works on reproducibility and model adoption patterns, and previously interned on an applied ML team where model choices were constrained by serving stacks and mobile inference settings.
members.private_state: He wants the project to feel genuinely different from existing activation-function surveys and to preserve the applied angle by reflecting what production teams actually ship, even if the evidence is messier than benchmark papers.
hidden_assumptions: If they say 'practice', it primarily means production-facing usage signals such as deployed model cards, framework defaults, inference libraries, and applied engineering writeups rather than research codebases.
A 'trend' can reasonably mean the current pattern of adoption across domains and stacks, even without a time-series reconstruction.
A paper is 'novel' only if it captures real-world constraints behind activation choices, including quantization, kernel support, and latency-sensitive deployment considerations.
When someone proposes a 'small empirical check', that means non-benchmark validation such as inspecting framework defaults or implementation support rather than retraining many models.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They repeatedly say the paper should compare research trends with practice.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means 'practice' as patterns visible in public open-source codebases, benchmark repos, and commonly reused training implementations.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means 'practice' as production-oriented adoption reflected in deployed systems, model cards, serving libraries, mobile/edge stacks, and engineering blogposts.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both interpretations are plausible within ML and both contrast naturally with 'research papers', so the phrase feels shared and no one hears an obvious contradiction in a brainstorming conversation.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the survey needs a novel angle rather than another catalog of activation functions.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks novelty comes from a systematic longitudinal synthesis with a clean taxonomy and modest empirical sanity checks.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks novelty comes from surfacing production constraints and adoption frictions that prior surveys ignored, even if the evidence is less standardized.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In brainstorming, 'novel angle' sounds like shared enthusiasm for differentiation; each person hears a compatible but different standard for what would impress reviewers.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss doing a trend analysis of activation-function usage.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes trend analysis means measuring change over time, such as year-by-year prevalence from 2018 to 2025.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes trend analysis can mean a present-day cross-sectional map of which activations dominate different application settings and deployment regimes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both temporal and cross-sectional summaries are commonly called 'trends' in survey writing, and neither interpretation sounds odd enough to trigger clarification during an idea-generation meeting.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree it would help to add a small validation study so the paper is not purely descriptive.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 imagines rerunning a few representative architectures with swapped activations under fixed training settings to test whether defaults drive reported choices.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 imagines a lightweight implementation audit, checking which activations are first-class citizens in major frameworks and inference toolchains, without substantial retraining.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both options are low-cost add-ons that could plausibly be called a 'small validation study', and in a fast brainstorm each person assumes the exact mode will be obvious later.

turns.inner_thought: We need something that reads as a methods-oriented synthesis, not another activation-function survey that just lists ReLU, GELU, Swish, Mish, and so on. If we frame it as comparing trends in research and practice, I can mine papers plus public codebases and model repos without needing any industry access. The trend analysis should really be temporal, ideally year-by-year, so it looks rigorous. And the novel angle has to be systematic enough for workshop reviewers to see a contribution beyond narrative commentary.
turns.utterance: Okay, so for this workshop paper, I think the key is to sharpen the angle fast. We should compare activation-function trends in research and practice, but without sliding into a generic catalog. And I do think the survey needs a novel angle rather than another list of functions and claimed pros and cons.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, exactly, but only if 'practice' means what teams actually ship rather than what shows up in academic training repos. The interesting story is that papers keep rotating through supposedly better activations, while deployed systems often stay with boring defaults because stacks, tooling, and latency constraints dominate. That gap is what would make it feel genuinely different from prior surveys.
turns.utterance: Yeah, I think the promising hook is to explain why the activations that dominate in practice do not always line up with what recent papers say is best. If we can make that contrast concrete, then it already feels more useful than a standard survey.

turns.inner_thought: I should steer this toward something we can execute cleanly: a trend analysis over the last several years, probably 2018 onward, using major public repositories and release code. That gives us a longitudinal story and avoids messy claims about real-world deployment we can't verify at scale. If we show when GELU displaced ReLU in transformers or when Swish-like families briefly surged, that's a publishable synthesis.
turns.utterance: One way to structure it is around a trend analysis of activation-function usage over the last several years. We could show when newer families gained traction, when some plateaued, and how that compares across major model implementations.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds good, though for me the trend analysis should really capture where ReLU-like choices still dominate in production-facing settings today. The reason is often not that people think ReLU is scientifically best; it's that deployment habits, operator support, and kernels keep it sticky. If we don't include that, the paper risks becoming just a polished repo-mining exercise.
turns.utterance: I like that. I’d just want the trend analysis to also capture where the more conventional choices keep persisting in practice, because a lot of the time the reasons are not the same reasons that show up in papers. That could be part of the novel angle rather than just reporting who proposed what.

turns.inner_thought: Good, we're aligned: systematic taxonomy plus evidence from literature and public implementations. If I pair paper claims with what people actually use in open-source training code, reviewers will see a rigorous synthesis. The novelty can come from organizing claim types—accuracy gains, optimization stability, efficiency rhetoric—and contrasting those with observed adoption patterns over time.
turns.utterance: Right, and I think the novel part could be a systematic taxonomy that pairs literature claims with what people actually use. That way reviewers see more than another activation-function survey; they see a structured comparison between research and practice.

turns.inner_thought: I’m glad she said novelty, because I need this not to become a polished catalog of paper claims and GitHub frequencies. To be genuinely novel, we have to foreground deployment constraints—quantization friendliness, operator availability, latency tradeoffs, implementation friction. Those are exactly the reasons applied teams ignore some academically popular activations.
turns.utterance: Agreed. For it to feel genuinely novel, I think we should foreground the practical constraints behind those choices rather than mainly listing accuracy deltas. Otherwise the comparison between research and practice may still feel too close to existing surveys.

turns.inner_thought: We’ll need something empirical so the paper isn't purely descriptive. A small validation study could be a few controlled reruns: same architecture, same recipe, swap activations, see whether some reported gains wash out when defaults are standardized. That is lightweight enough for the lab in a week or two and helps support the claim that many choices are inherited rather than actively tuned.
turns.utterance: I also think it would help to add a small validation study so the paper is not purely descriptive. Maybe we can use it to test whether some of the claimed gains are more fragile than they look once settings are held fixed.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, a small validation study would be great, but I really want that to stay lightweight and implementation-facing. We could audit support and friction across major frameworks and toolchains, which directly validates the practice side of the story. I definitely do not want this turning into a retraining-heavy benchmark mini-project.
turns.utterance: Yeah, I’m on board with a small validation study. If we keep it lightweight, it could really strengthen the paper and make the research-versus-practice comparison feel grounded rather than purely observational.

turns.inner_thought: For evidence, the scalable core is obvious: papers, official release code, and popular GitHub implementations. That gives us enough coverage to characterize practice in a way we can defend. I should keep the source list bounded so this doesn't balloon into a qualitative industry ethnography.
turns.utterance: On sources, I’m thinking papers, release code, and widely used public implementations are probably the backbone. That should already give us enough to map practice against research in a reasonably systematic way.

turns.inner_thought: That’s a start, but if the practice side is only public implementations, we’ll miss the actual deployed story. I should push for model cards, serving documentation, and engineering writeups without making it sound like a disagreement. Those are messy, but they’re exactly where current adoption and constraints become visible.
turns.utterance: Makes sense. I’d also add model cards, serving docs, and engineering writeups, so the practice side reflects what teams really use and not only what shows up alongside release code.

turns.inner_thought: Fine, as long as the main analysis stays clean. The trend analysis should still be summarized year by year; that gives the paper a crisp visual story. Then we can interpret why certain activations plateau despite strong claims in the literature. That kind of longitudinal plot will make the synthesis feel methodical rather than anecdotal.
turns.utterance: Yes, and I think we can probably summarize the main trend analysis with year-by-year uptake plots, then use the discussion to explain why some activations plateau even when paper results look strong.

turns.inner_thought: Year-by-year is fine, but I also want a present-day map across domains and deployment contexts, because that’s what practitioners care about. Vision, NLP, edge, maybe server-side inference—show what dominates where. To me that still fits under trend analysis, and it makes the paper actionable.
turns.utterance: I’d love to pair that with a domain-by-domain snapshot too—vision, language, maybe edge-oriented settings—so the trend analysis is also useful for someone trying to choose an activation today, not just read a historical story.

turns.inner_thought: Good, I can work with that language. I’ll draft the taxonomy and validation framing around controlled checks, and Leo can start compiling the practice evidence from the various public sources. I’m assuming he’ll pull together repos and implementations first, which is exactly what we need to move quickly.
turns.utterance: Okay, that sounds like a workable split. Why don’t you start compiling the practice evidence, and I’ll draft the taxonomy and the validation section framing so we have a sharper concept before the end of the week.

turns.inner_thought: Great. I’ll gather current adoption signals and implementation support across the production-facing sources I care about, and that should make the gap very visible. By next meeting I want enough material to show why some activations look good in papers but still don't win in deployed settings.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I’ll gather signals on current adoption and implementation support so when we reconvene we should have a clearer picture of the research-versus-practice gap and what the trend analysis can actually support.
